full_judgment:
3. The pre-emptor's case, in short, is that the case land originally belonged to Dianat Ullah and Kudrat Ali Sheikh under CS Khatian No. 129 Dianat Ullah died leaving 2 sons Garibullah and Efatullah and 3 daughters Kadiman, Durjaton and Kajiman, Kudrat Ali died leaving behind 5 sons Mir Ali, Ser Ali, Asgar Ali, Alinoor and Md Rahmat and 4 daughters Basiran, Joyton, Jiraton and Eaton. The land of Plot No. 306 was amicably partitioned, Kefatullah, son of Dianat Ullah obtained 54 decimals and Asgar Ali, son of Kudrat Ullah obtained 54 decimals out of 108 decimals of land, Kefatullah sold his land to one Abdul Halim and then he sold the land to Mvi Ramijuddin Ahmed and he sold the land on 30-12-1974 to the petitioner. Asgar Ali sold his land to one Matiar Rahman and Abdul Basir Khan, Matiar Rahman Khan sold the larid to the petitioner and opposite party Nos. 6 and 8. The petitioner is entitled to file the pre-emption case. The co-sharer of the land opposite party Nos. 2-5 sold the land to the opposite party No.1 on 21-10-1993 collusively and they did not serve any notice of transfer to the petitioner. On 12-2-1996 the petitioner came to know of the transfer through Mohiruddin. The petitioner obtained the certified copy of the transfer deed on 19-2-96 and filed the pre-emption case within the period of limitation from the date of knowledge. The opposite party No. 1, the pre-emptee purchaser, appeared and filed written objection stating that the pre-emptor-petitioner is not the co-sharer of the jote and the land belongs to a separate holding. Genealogy of CS Khatian is wrong and the case is not maintainable and that the preemptor did not mention how much land he possesses and, as such, the case is barred under section 90 of the State Acquisition arid Tenancy Act. The pre-emptee-opposite party No. 1 further state that he is a very poor man and he was a servant of the local Chairman who out of pity managed the service of the pre-emptee in Malaysia and while he was in Malaysia he has purchased 27 decimals of land on 21-10-1993. He further submits that before his purchase, the transferor requested the pre-emptor to purchase the land but he refused. The consideration money was paid to the transferor through Md Fazlur Rahman, the local Union Parishad Chairman. The pre-emptor was in full knowledge regarding the transfer. After the purchase the father of the pre-emptee possessed the land on behalf of the pre-emptee and afterwards the pre-emptee himself is possessing the land. The pre-emptor had a knowledge as to the sale and delivery of possession of the land. Since the value of the land has been increased; the pre-emptor fi led the instant pre-emption case after several years. The pre-emptee has developed the land by investing an amount of Taka 5000 and, as such, the pre-emption case is liable to be dismissed. 

 10. The learned Advocate for the pre-emptor-petitioner submits that both the Courts below found that the pre-emptor is a co-sharer and entitled to preempt the case holding and that there is no defect of party and there is no development of the case land after the purchase. Both the Courts below also held that no notice was served upon the pre-emptor regarding the transfer and that the pre-emptor has no land more than the ceiling as contemplated under section 90 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 11. The trial Court found that the case has been filed within the period of limitation but the appellate Court on misreading of evidence allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment and order of the trial Court only on the point of limitation disbelieving the date of knowledge of the pre-emptor. During his argument he has referred the case of Hajera Bibi vs Noor Jahan Begum reported in 35 DLR 338, Jafar Ali vs Husier Ali and others reported in 46 DLR (AD) 187 and Dalilur Rahman vs Syed Omar reported in 5 MLR (AD) 24. He has also pointed out the relevant portion of the evidence on record stating that PW 1, the pre-emptor, informed by PW 2 Mohiruddin about the transfer on 12-2-1996 at about 12-30 hours PW 2 Mohiruddin, who is an illiterate cultivator, has stated that he has informed the pre-emptor regarding the transfer on the same day but did not state the date of his information. The learned Counsel further submits that the pre-emptee gave no suggestion that the preemptor was aware of the sale on such and such date. Rather DW 2 Kalimuddin, father of the pre-emptee, has admitted that they did not inform the pre-emptor about the sale. DW 5 Fazlur Rahman who is the negotiator and Chairman has admitted that the pre- emptor was not aware of the sale: Admittedly, the pre-emptee DW 1 Hosain Ali was not present at the time of purchase of the case land and his father DW 2 Kalimuddin purchased the case land on his behalf and took possession. DW 2 Kalimuddin has stated that he was in possession for 4 years and then his son was possessing the land for 2 years and, as such, it appears that they were in possession for 6 years. The deposition was made in 1997. So, DW 2 Kalimuddin is in possession from 1991 long before purchase of the land in 1993. Both the Courts below disbelieved the development of the land by investing Taka 5000. DW 2 Kalimuddin and DW 5 Fazlur Rahman has admitted that PW 1 Abdur Rashid Miah pre-emptor was not aware of the transfer. Admittedly, no notice of transfer was served upon the pre-emptor. In the case of Hajera Khatun vs Noor Jahan Begum reported in 35 DLR 238 it has been held that when no notice of transfer is served on the co-sharer, onus of proving date of transfer does not lie on the co-sharer. It appears that the pre-emptee was in possession long before the transfer and, as such, none could know of the transfer of the case land. It has been held in the case of Dalilur Rahman vs Syed Nor and others reported in 5 MLR (AD) 24 that the pre-emptor had no means to know about the transfer if the purchaser is in possession of the case land before the purchase as mortgagee or bargader. 

 14. Regarding the point of limitation, he has submitted that the date of knowledge as stated by the pre-emptor has not been corroborated by any legal evidence. During his argument he has cited the case of Jitendra Nath Howlader vs Bisheshwar Howlader reported in 42 DLR 253 wherein it has been held that the date of knowledge about the sale of the land under pre-emption is a finding of fact and unless the finding suffers from infirmity or its perverse, the High Court Division will not interfere with the finding of the lower appellate Court in its jurisdiction. He also pointed out the relevant portion on the evidences on record that PW 1 Abdur Rashid Miah has stated that PW 2 Mohiruddin on 12-2-1996 has informed him about the transfer. But PW 2 Mohiruddin gave no specific date, only stating that on the same day he informed PW 1 Abdur Rashid Miah about the transfer of the case land. 

 15. It appears that PW 2 Mohiruddin is an illiterate cultivator and it is not possible for him to give and remember any specific date. He has stated that as and when he heard about the transfer then and there he informed the matter to the pre-emptor. The pre-emptee did not specifically challenge the date of knowledge of the pre-emptor by giving any specific date or by ascertaining any other means of his knowledge. Rather the father of the pre-emptee has stated that they did not inform the pre-emptor. PW 5 Fazlur Rahman, the local Chairman and negotiator of the transfer, specifically stated that Abdur Rashid Miah pre-emptor was not aware of the transfer and, as such, the finding of the date of knowledge as has been found by the appellate Court are perverse and not based on evidence on record. In the, case of Jafar Ali vs Hushier Ali and others reported in 46 DLR (AD) 187 it has been held that if there being no evidence on record challenging the date of knowledge of the pre-emptor about the transfer of the land, the contention that the application is barred by limitation is untenable in law.
